entities.name: Alexander of Hierapolis
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alexander of Hierapolis, bishop of Hierapolis Bambyce in Roman Syria during the early 5th century CE, emerged as a principal defender of Antiochene Christology and a staunch opponent of Cyril of Alexandria's theological formulations. His significance is rooted in his pivotal, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, resistance to the decisions of the Council of Ephesus in 431 CE, which condemned Nestorius. Alexander represented a theological tradition emphasizing the distinctness of Christ's divine and human natures, a perspective that ultimately contributed to the enduring schism between the mainstream Chalcedonian church and the Church of the East.

At the Council of Ephesus, convened by Emperor Theodosius II, Alexander vigorously supported Nestorius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, against Cyril's anathemas. He, alongside John of Antioch and other Eastern bishops, arrived late and subsequently held a counter-council, refusing to acknowledge Nestorius's deposition or the condemnation of his teachings. This defiance led to his own deposition and subsequent exile, initially to the mining region of Famothis in Egypt, and later to various locations on Rhodes, as decreed by imperial edict in 432 CE. Despite his personal hardship, Alexander maintained an extensive correspondence, notably with Theodoret of Cyrrhus, reaffirming his commitment to the Antiochene creed and criticizing the Cyrilline formula 'Theotokos' (God-bearer) as applied to Mary.
